pll1d1c3-d1e3473.summary: Introduces a second Augustinian definition from De Trinitate X: to use is to take something into the faculty of the will; to enjoy is to use with joy not of hope but of the reality. So every enjoyer uses, but not every user enjoys.
claims: Use is taking something into the faculty of the will.
Enjoyment is use with the joy of possession, not of hope.
All who enjoy use, but not all who use enjoy.

pll1d1c3-d1e3498.summary: Raises the difficulty that this definition implies we do not enjoy in this life, where we rejoice only in hope, contradicting the earlier definition under which many cling to God here.
claims: The two Augustinian definitions appear to conflict about enjoyment in this life.

pll1d1c3-d1e3504.summary: Resolves the conflict: we enjoy both now and hereafter, but in heaven properly, perfectly, and fully by sight, and here less fully while walking in hope.
claims: We enjoy God both in this life and in the future life.
Enjoyment is full and proper only in the vision of heaven.

pll1d1c3-d1e3507.summary: Supports the resolution with Augustine's statement that we enjoy known things in which the will rests.
claims: Enjoyment requires knowledge and resting of the will.

pll1d1c3-d1e3533.summary: Adds Augustine: angels already enjoy God and are blessed; we enjoy him partly in this life through a mirror and in an enigma, which makes our pilgrimage more bearable and our desire for its end stronger.
claims: The angels already enjoy God and are blessed.
In this life we enjoy God partially, through a mirror and in an enigma.

pll1d1c3-d1e3558.summary: Gives an alternative resolution: one who enjoys in this life has joy not only of hope but of the reality, since delighting in the beloved already holds it in some measure. Concludes that God is to be enjoyed, not used.
claims: Present delight in God is a partial possession of him.
God is to be enjoyed, not used.

pll1d1c3-d1e3575.summary: With Augustine, distinguishes proper from loose enjoyment: 'enjoy' is often used for using with delight, but if one passes through the delight and refers it to the abiding end, one uses it; to enjoy truly is to rest one's joy finally, which is to be done only in the Trinity.
claims: We enjoy properly only what makes us blessed.
Delight referred beyond itself is use, not enjoyment in the proper sense.
Final rest of joy belongs only to the Trinity, the supreme unchangeable good.

pll1d1c3-d1e3612.summary: Poses the next question: since humans who enjoy and use are themselves things, should they enjoy one another, use one another, or both?

pll1d1c3-d1e3626.summary: Answers with Augustine: a human is to be loved for the sake of something else, since the blessed life lies in what is loved for itself, and hope is not to be placed in man (Jer 17:5). So no one should enjoy even himself.
claims: A human being is to be loved for the sake of something else.
Hope must not be placed in a human being.
No one should enjoy himself.

pll1d1c3-d1e3661.summary: Raises an objection from Paul's letter to Philemon, 'Thus, brother, I will enjoy you in the Lord,' which seems to permit enjoying a human.

pll1d1c3-d1e3680.summary: Resolves the objection with Augustine: by adding 'in the Lord' Paul placed the end of his love in God. Enjoying a human in God is enjoying God rather than the human.
claims: To enjoy a human in God is to enjoy God rather than the human.

pll1d1c3-d1e3728.summary: Turns to God's love for us. Augustine asks whether God loves us as one who uses or enjoys. He cannot enjoy us, since that would imply he needs our good, so he 'uses' us, but not as we use things: he refers his use of us to his own goodness and has mercy on us so that we may enjoy him, while our mercy to others is rewarded by enjoyment of God.
claims: God does not enjoy us, since he needs no good of ours.
God uses us, referring this use to his goodness.
God's mercy toward us aims at our enjoying him.
Mercy shown to others is rewarded with the enjoyment of God.

pll1d1c3-d1e3748.summary: Completes the account: we exist because God is good and are good insofar as we exist; because he is just we are not evil with impunity, and insofar as evil we exist less. God's use of us is for our benefit and refers only to his goodness.
claims: Our being and goodness derive from God's goodness.
Insofar as we are evil we exist less.
God's use of us benefits us and is referred to his goodness, not his utility.

pll1d1c3-d1e3760.summary: Raises a new question: whether virtues are to be used or enjoyed.

pll1d1c3-d1e3763.summary: First opinion: virtues are to be used and not enjoyed, on Augustine's authority that only the Trinity, the supreme unchangeable good, is to be enjoyed.
claims: Only the supreme unchangeable good is to be enjoyed, hence not virtues.

pll1d1c3-d1e3770.summary: Further argument for the first opinion: virtues are loved for eternal beatitude, not for themselves, while whatever is enjoyed must be loved for its own sake.
claims: What is enjoyed must be loved for its own sake.
Virtues are loved for the sake of beatitude.

pll1d1c3-d1e3775.summary: Supports the claim that virtues are loved only for beatitude with De Trinitate XIII: if beatitude is not loved, the virtues loved for its sake cease to be loved. Hence virtues are not to be enjoyed.
claims: Virtues are loved for the sake of beatitude alone.
Therefore virtues are not to be enjoyed.

pll1d1c3-d1e3797.summary: Contrary opinion: virtues are to be enjoyed because they are sought and loved for their own sake, which is supported by Ambrose on Galatians 5:22, where the works of the Spirit are called 'fruits' because they are sought for themselves.
claims: Virtues are sought for their own sake and so are to be enjoyed.
The Spirit's gifts are called fruits because they are desired for themselves.

pll1d1c3-d1e3824.summary: Lombard's resolution of the conflicting authorities: virtues are to be sought and loved for their own sake, since they give their possessors holy delight, and yet for beatitude alone, because love must not stop there but be referred to the supreme good, the final end.
claims: Virtues are loved for their own sake, since they give holy delight.
Virtues are also loved for the sake of beatitude alone.
Love must be referred beyond virtues to the supreme good, the final end.

pll1d1c3-d1e3827.summary: Explains Augustine's 'for beatitude alone': it does not deny that we love virtues for themselves, but means that we refer this love to the supreme good, in which alone we rest. Hence virtues are not to be enjoyed.
claims: Loving virtues for their own sake is compatible with referring that love to God.
Virtues are not to be enjoyed.

pll1d1c3-d1e3836.summary: Anticipates an objection: if enjoyment is clinging to a thing for its own sake, and virtues are loved for their own sake, virtues should be enjoyed.

pll1d1c3-d1e3839.summary: Replies that 'for its own sake' in the definition means for its own sake alone, without reference to another, with the end placed there. Hence virtues are to be used and through them the supreme good is enjoyed, and the same holds of the good will.
claims: 'For its own sake' in the definition of enjoyment means 'for its own sake alone'.
We use virtues and through them enjoy the supreme good.
The same applies to the good will.

pll1d1c3-d1e3855.summary: With Augustine's 'the will is that by which we enjoy,' extends the point: we enjoy through virtues, not the virtues themselves, unless some virtue is God, as charity, to be treated later.
claims: We enjoy through the will and the virtues, not the virtues themselves.
If a virtue were God, as charity is, it would be enjoyed.

pll1d1c3-d1e3874.summary: Summarizes the distinction: things are to be enjoyed, to be used, or enjoy and use; among things to be used are some through which we enjoy, such as virtues and the soul's powers, which are natural goods. Announces that before signs the treatise will first consider the things to be enjoyed, the holy and undivided Trinity.
claims: Among things to be used are virtues and powers of the soul, through which we enjoy.
The treatise will first consider the Trinity.

pl-l1d1c3.summary: Works through three difficulties about enjoyment and use. (1) Augustine's second definition (enjoyment as use with joy of the reality, not of hope) seems to exclude enjoyment in this life; Lombard answers that we enjoy here imperfectly and in heaven fully. (2) Whether humans are to be enjoyed or used: Augustine says neither ourselves nor others are to be enjoyed for their own sake; 'I will enjoy you in the Lord' (Philemon) means enjoying God in the neighbor; God does not enjoy us but 'uses' us for our benefit and his goodness. (3) Whether virtues are to be enjoyed: Lombard reconciles Augustine and Ambrose by holding that virtues are loved for their own sake yet referred to beatitude, so they are used and through them, as through the good will, God is enjoyed, unless a virtue is God himself, as charity. Concludes with a summary and the transition to the Trinity.
claims: We enjoy God in this life in hope and imperfectly, and in the next life fully and properly.
God alone is to be enjoyed; humans are not to be enjoyed for their own sake, not even oneself.
To enjoy someone 'in the Lord' is to enjoy God rather than the human.
God does not enjoy us but uses us, referring our use to his goodness and our benefit.
Virtues are loved for their own sake and yet for beatitude alone; they are used, and through them we enjoy the supreme good.
The treatise will next treat the things to be enjoyed, namely the Trinity.
concepts: enjoyment in hope vs in reality
